Rain Down the Drain

Germany · Frankfurt am Main · 2026

Rain down the drain

This year is short on rain, yet we flush our toilets with drinking water. Meanwhile, the rain on Frankfurt’s roofs runs into the downpipes. Here is how much water that is.

77%of normal precipitation fell in Germany in January–September 2026
27%of household drinking water is used to flush toilets
≈11 million m³of rainwater runs off Frankfurt’s roofs in a normal year

1 · Rainfall

2026 is a dry year

From January to September, Germany received an average of 455 mm of precipitation. The normal for these months (1991–2020) is 594 mm. Only February was wetter than usual; July brought half the normal amount.

An important caveat. Over 145 years of records, Germany’s annual precipitation has not declined: the linear trend since 1881 is slightly positive (about +4 mm per decade). The problem is different: recent years have included several very dry ones. 2018 was the 4th driest of 145 years, 2025 the 15th and 2022 the 25th. And 2026 is running well below normal so far.

2 · Water use

We flush toilets with drinking water

In 2023, a person in Germany used an average of 121 litres of tap water a day, all of it drinking quality. More than a quarter goes to flushing toilets: about 33 litres a day, or 12 m³ per person a year. Rainwater would do the job just as well.

There is a separate estimate for Frankfurt. According to a study reported by the trade journal ZfK in 2022, households use about 118 litres per person per day, and 33% of that (39 litres) could be replaced with non-potable water, for example for flushing toilets and watering gardens.

3 · Frankfurt

A third of the city is sealed by asphalt, concrete and roofs

Copernicus satellite data show that 33.7% of Frankfurt’s area is sealed. That is about 84 km² out of 248 km². Water cannot soak through these surfaces into the ground.

The average hides a sharp contrast. Half of the area (the city forest in the south, fields, parks) is not sealed at all, while almost a quarter is 80% sealed or more.

Roofs were counted separately. Building footprints from OpenStreetMap add up to 25 km², or 10% of the city. Roofs are what feed the downpipes, and their water is the cleanest.

4 · Rain over Frankfurt

Frankfurt got 6.5 mm of rain in July 2026

Frankfurt gets 637 mm a year on average, less than the German average (792 mm). From January to September 2026 it received 361 mm, 77% of normal. July brought 6.5 mm against a normal of 66.5 mm.

5 · The balance

Roofs shed about as much water as homes could replace

Take a normal year (637 mm). One millimetre of rain on one square kilometre is 1,000 m³ of water. Some rain evaporates or is held on the roof, so roughly 50–80% reaches the pipes. The calculation uses 70%.

In a normal year, about 11 million m³ runs off Frankfurt’s roofs: roughly 40 litres per resident per day. That is almost exactly the amount of drinking water households could replace with non-potable water (11 million m³), and more than goes to flushing toilets (9 million m³). Whatever is not collected or absorbed on site goes into the sewer.

6 · No storage, no supply

Rain doesn’t fall when you need it

Month by month, the picture is uneven. In January and February 2026, the roofs would have delivered more than needed. In July, almost nothing. Rainwater has to be stored: in tanks under buildings or in shared neighbourhood reservoirs.

Takeaways

What this means

  1. Germany’s annual rainfall has not fallen over 145 years, but recent years have included several very dry ones. 2026 is 23% below normal so far.
  2. About a quarter of drinking water is flushed down the toilet. For Frankfurt, the share that could be replaced with non-potable water is estimated at a third.
  3. In a normal year, Frankfurt’s roofs shed about as much water as that replacement needs. Uncollected, it goes to the sewer.
  4. The main constraint is storage: rain falls unevenly, and July 2026 brought almost none.

Method and assumptions

  • Germany: DWD area averages (regional_averages_DE). Frankfurt: mean of DWD 1×1 km grid cells within the city boundary (from Germany_Gemeinde.geojson, AGS 06412000). DWD may still revise the September figures.
  • Sealing: Copernicus HRL Imperviousness Density 2018, 10 m, averaged over the city. An independent GDV estimate based on Urban Atlas 2012 gives 36.9%.
  • Roofs: total footprint area of OpenStreetMap buildings (data as of 1 June 2026), excluding underground structures. Missing buildings in OSM would make this an underestimate.
  • The 50–80% runoff coefficient is an assumption. A typical pitched roof is closer to 80%; gravel and green roofs are lower. Further losses in pipes are not modelled.
  • No open data was found on what share of sealed surfaces drains into the sewer. Rain on all sealed surfaces is therefore shown as an upper bound, not as the volume that reached the sewer.
  • Use: Mainova, about 48 million m³ a year (c. 2020, including businesses and commuters). The replaceable share (39 litres per day) comes from the study reported by ZfK.
